talk_about: Why is it useful for lions to live in a family instead of alone?
If you could hear something 5 miles away, what would you listen for?
Which other animal at the zoo lives in a family group?
push_further: A mane makes a male slower, hotter and more visible. Why hasn’t evolution removed it?
Lions and cheetahs share the same plains. How do they avoid competing directly?
Find one more animal on your zoo map that lives in a group. What does the group give it?

teach: A group of lions is a pride.
They live on grasslands / savannah, not jungle.
Their famous sound is a roar.
Male lions often grow a big mane.

questions.title: Family
questions.stem: What do you call a group of lions?
questions.why: Lions live together in a pride — a social group that shares space and raises cubs.

questions.title: Food
questions.stem: What do lions mostly eat?
questions.why: Lions eat meat. They mostly hunt hooved animals such as zebra, wildebeest, and antelope.

questions.title: Voice
questions.stem: What sound is a lion famous for?
questions.why: A lion’s roar can travel a long way — about 8 km / 5 miles (Wikipedia).

questions.title: Body
questions.stem: Which lion usually grows a big fluffy mane?
questions.why: Male lions often grow a big mane around the head and neck.

questions.title: Young
questions.stem: What is a baby lion called?
questions.why: A baby lion is a cub. Many cubs have faint spots that fade as they grow.

questions.title: Home
questions.stem: Where do wild lions mostly live?
questions.why: Wild lions mostly live on grassland, savannah, and shrubland — rarely in closed forest.

questions.title: Rest
questions.stem: How much of the day do lions often spend resting?
questions.why: Lions often rest or stay inactive for about 20 hours a day.

questions.title: Hunting
questions.stem: In a pride, who usually does most of the hunting?
questions.why: In a pride, lionesses usually do most of the hunting, often together.

questions.title: Body
questions.stem: What special tip does a lion’s tail have?
questions.why: A lion’s tail ends in a dark hairy tuft.

questions.title: Myth buster
questions.stem: Do lions really live in a jungle like in some cartoons?
questions.why: Cartoons show jungle lions, but wild lions mostly live on open grassland.

questions.title: Name
questions.stem: What is the lion’s scientific name?
questions.why: The lion is a large cat in the genus Panthera. Its scientific name is Panthera leo.

questions.title: Pride
questions.stem: In a typical pride, who forms the stable core?
questions.why: A pride’s stable core is related females and cubs. Adult males are usually unrelated to those females.

questions.title: Prey
questions.stem: What do wild lions mostly hunt?
choices: Tiny prey like hares and monkeys
questions.why: Lions mostly hunt medium-sized and large hooved mammals such as zebra, wildebeest, and buffalo — not tiny prey as their main diet.

questions.title: Speed
questions.stem: How do lions usually chase prey?
choices: Long stamina runs for many miles
Short fast bursts of about 30–37 mph
questions.why: Lions have quick burst speed of about 48–59 km/h (30–37 mph) but little stamina, so they do not run long chases.

questions.title: Status
questions.stem: How does the IUCN list wild lions today?
questions.why: Lions have been listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. African populations have declined sharply in recent decades.

questions.title: Range
questions.stem: Where do wild Asiatic lions live today?
choices: Mainly Gir National Park in western India
questions.why: Wild Asiatic lions today survive mainly in and around Gir National Park in Gujarat, western India.

questions.title: Cubs
questions.stem: When can a newborn lion cub see?
choices: It is born with eyes already open
Eyes open around a week after birth
Eyes stay closed for a year
questions.why: Lion cubs are born blind. Their eyes open around seven days after birth.

questions.title: Birth
questions.stem: About how long is a lioness’s pregnancy, and how many cubs are usual?
choices: About two years; one cub only
questions.why: Gestation is about 110 days. A litter is often between one and four cubs.

questions.title: Takeover
questions.stem: What often happens to young cubs when new males take over a pride?
choices: The new males adopt every cub
The new males often kill existing young cubs
Cubs immediately leave to hunt alone
questions.why: When new males oust the previous males, they often kill existing young cubs. Females then become ready to mate sooner.

questions.title: Color
questions.stem: What makes a white lion white?
choices: It is a true albino with pink eyes
A rare pale morph from leucism, with normal eye and skin pigment
questions.why: White lions are a rare pale morph caused by leucism, not true albinism. They still have normal pigmentation in the eyes and skin.

questions.title: Roar
questions.stem: What helps a lion roar, unlike a house cat’s continuous purr?
choices: A fully stiff hyoid bone like a house cat
A stretchy hyoid ligament (not a fully stiff bone)
questions.why: One reason lions can roar is a stretchy hyoid ligament in the throat — not a fully stiff bone like a house cat. They do not make a house cat’s continuous purr.

questions.title: Scent
questions.stem: When a lion curls its lips in a flehmen grimace, where does the scent go?
questions.why: The flehmen face (open mouth, wrinkled nose) helps a lion sniff chemical signals. The lip-curl routes scent toward the vomeronasal organ, a special smell sensor.

questions.title: Teeth
questions.stem: What are a lion’s carnassial teeth built to do?
choices: Shear meat with blade-like cheek teeth (upper P4 / lower m1)
questions.why: Carnassials are blade-like cheek teeth — the upper fourth premolar and lower first molar — that shear meat.

questions.title: Species
questions.stem: Which two living lion subspecies do scientists recognize today?
choices: Panthera leo leo and Panthera leo melanochaita
questions.why: In 2017 the Cat Specialist Group recognized two living subspecies: P. l. leo and P. l. melanochaita. Cave lions and American lions are extinct relatives, not living subspecies.

questions.title: Tail
questions.stem: What can hide inside a lion’s dark tail tuft?
choices: A small hard spur; its function is unknown
A second claw used for climbing
questions.why: In some lions the dark tail tuft hides a small hard spur. Wikipedia notes its function is unknown.

questions.title: Takeover
questions.stem: Why do new males often kill young cubs after taking over a pride?
choices: So females return to estrus and can mate sooner
questions.why: Females usually do not become ready to mate again until their cubs grow up or die. Killing young cubs often brings females back into estrus sooner.

questions.title: Society
questions.stem: How do lions compare with other wild cats?
choices: They are the most social of wild cats, living in prides
They are the only cats that never meet
They are less social than typical solitary big cats
questions.why: The lion is the most social of all wild felid species. Related females and cubs form a pride — unlike typical solitary big cats.

questions.title: Decline
questions.stem: What are the greatest causes for concern in the lion’s decline?
choices: Habitat loss and conflict with people
Lions moving to the deep ocean
questions.why: The exact drop is not fully understood, but habitat loss and conflicts with people are the greatest concerns. Lions are still listed as Vulnerable.

questions.title: Muscle
questions.stem: Why do lions hunt with short rushes instead of long chases?
choices: They have a high share of fast-twitch muscle and little stamina
questions.why: Lion muscle has a high concentration of fast-twitch fibers, so they can sprint in short bursts but have little stamina.

questions.title: Rivals
questions.stem: How do lions and spotted hyenas treat each other’s kills?
choices: They steal kills from each other (kleptoparasitism both ways)
questions.why: Lions and spotted hyenas compete for prey and carrion. Each species may steal the other’s kills — kleptoparasitism goes both ways.

reticulated-giraffe.source_note: Facts from Wikipedia, Giraffe / Reticulated giraffe.
talk_about: Why might a long neck help a giraffe besides reaching high leaves?
If you stood as tall as a giraffe, what would you notice first at the zoo?
Which other animal at the zoo has a special tongue or a long neck?
push_further: A giraffe must spread its front legs to drink. What risk could that pose in the wild?
Each giraffe’s spots are unique. How could that help a keeper tell them apart?
Find one more animal on your zoo map that eats leaves from trees. How does it reach them?

teach: The giraffe is the tallest living land animal.
It eats leaves and shoots from tall trees.
A very long neck helps it reach high foliage.
A baby giraffe is a calf.
Wild giraffes live on African savannah and open woodland.

questions.title: Tallest
questions.stem: What record does a giraffe hold among living land animals?
questions.why: The giraffe is the tallest living land animal — taller than any other animal that lives on land today.

questions.title: Food
questions.stem: What do giraffes mostly eat?
choices: Leaves and shoots from tall trees
questions.why: Giraffes eat leaves and shoots from tall trees, especially acacia. They are not meat-eaters.

questions.title: Neck
questions.stem: Why does a giraffe have such a long neck?
choices: To store water like a camel
questions.why: A giraffe’s extremely long neck helps it reach high foliage that shorter animals cannot.

questions.title: Tongue
questions.stem: What is special about a giraffe’s tongue?
choices: It is very long and dark, for stripping leaves
It is forked like a snake
It is short and used only to drink
questions.why: A giraffe uses a very long, dark tongue to pull and strip leaves from thorny branches.

questions.title: Young
questions.stem: What is a baby giraffe called, and what can it do soon after birth?
choices: A cub — it stays lying down for weeks
A calf — it can stand soon after birth
A chick — it hatches from an egg
questions.why: A baby giraffe is a calf. Newborns can stand soon after they are born.

questions.title: Home
questions.stem: Where do wild giraffes mostly live?
questions.why: Wild giraffes live on African savannah and open woodland — not only one country.

questions.title: Drink
questions.stem: How does a giraffe drink water?
choices: It spreads its front legs or bends its knees
questions.why: A giraffe’s neck and legs are so long that it spreads its front legs or bends its knees to reach the water.

questions.title: Ossicones
questions.stem: What are the horn-like bumps on a giraffe’s head?
choices: Antlers that fall off each year
questions.why: Those bumps are ossicones — skin-covered, horn-like knobs. They are not antlers that shed.

questions.title: Coat
questions.stem: What is special about a giraffe’s coat?
choices: Every giraffe has the same spots
Dark patches in a net-like pattern; each giraffe’s spots are unique
It is bright blue with stripes
questions.why: A reticulated giraffe’s dark patches look like a net. Each giraffe’s spot pattern is unique.

questions.title: Myth buster
questions.stem: Does a giraffe have extra neck bones compared with most mammals?
choices: No — still seven vertebrae, just much longer
questions.why: Like most mammals, a giraffe has seven neck vertebrae. Each bone is just much longer.

questions.title: Relatives
questions.stem: What is the giraffe’s closest living relative?
questions.why: Giraffes and the okapi are the only living members of family Giraffidae. The okapi is the giraffe’s closest living relative.

questions.title: Name
questions.stem: What does the old English name “camelopard” mean?
questions.why: “Camelopard” comes from Greek words for camel and leopard — a camel-like shape with leopard-like colouration.

questions.title: Ossicones
questions.stem: What are a giraffe’s ossicones made of?
choices: Ossified cartilage covered in skin and fused to the skull
questions.why: Ossicones form from ossified cartilage, stay covered in skin, and fuse to the skull. They are not antlers that shed.

questions.title: Necking
questions.stem: How do male giraffes usually fight to establish dominance?
choices: They swing their necks and land blows with ossicones
questions.why: Males “neck” — swinging their necks and trying to land blows with their ossicones to decide who is dominant.

questions.title: Speed
questions.stem: How fast can a giraffe gallop in a short burst?
choices: Faster than a cheetah for hours
questions.why: Giraffes can gallop roughly 30–37 mph in short bursts. They are not built for long, all-day chases.

questions.title: Ruminate
questions.stem: How does a giraffe chew its food a second time?
choices: It never chews again after the first swallow
It has a four-chambered stomach and brings cud back up the long neck
It stores food in its ossicones
questions.why: Giraffes are ruminants with a four-chambered stomach. Strong oesophageal muscles send cud back up the long neck to be chewed again.

questions.title: Sleep
questions.stem: How do giraffes usually sleep?
choices: They sleep about 20 hours a day like lions
In short bouts that add up to only a few hours a day
questions.why: Giraffes sleep in short, interrupted bouts that total only a few hours a day — not one long night of sleep.

questions.title: Calves
questions.stem: How tall is a newborn giraffe, and how soon can it run?
choices: Mouse-sized; it cannot walk for months
Already about as tall as a person, and it can run within hours
Taller than an adult giraffe on day one
questions.why: A newborn calf is already about as tall as a person. Within a few hours it can run, though it still hides a lot in the first weeks.

questions.title: Threats
questions.stem: What are the main threats to wild giraffes today?
choices: Habitat loss and hunting for bushmeat
Giraffes moving to the deep ocean
questions.why: The biggest concerns are habitat loss and killing for bushmeat. Exact IUCN labels have shifted as giraffe species were split.

questions.title: Tongue
questions.stem: Why might a giraffe’s tongue be dark?
choices: The dark colour may help protect it from sunburn while browsing
questions.why: A giraffe’s tongue is dark — Wikipedia notes it is black, perhaps to protect against sunburn while the animal browses in the sun.

questions.title: Species
questions.stem: How do many scientists treat living giraffes today?
choices: Always one species forever, with no debate
Often as several species (often four); the reticulated giraffe is Giraffa reticulata
Only as two extinct fossil species
questions.why: Giraffes were long treated as one species. Many researchers now recognize several living species — often four — and the reticulated giraffe as Giraffa reticulata. Wikipedia treats that recognition as ongoing debate, not a forever rule.

questions.title: Heart
questions.stem: Why must a giraffe’s heart work so hard to supply the brain?
choices: The heart is tiny and barely beats
It must generate roughly double typical human blood pressure to push blood up the long neck
Giraffes have no blood vessels in the neck
questions.why: Wikipedia says the giraffe heart must generate about double the blood pressure a human needs to keep blood flowing to the brain. Exact pressure readings vary, so we keep the “roughly double” idea.

questions.title: Circulation
questions.stem: What helps protect a giraffe’s brain when the head drops to drink?
choices: A rete mirabile in the neck plus valves in the jugular veins
questions.why: When the head lowers, a rete mirabile — a net of vessels in the upper neck — plus valves in the jugular veins keep too much blood from flooding the brain.

questions.title: Neck bones
questions.stem: How is a giraffe’s neck built, compared with most other mammals?
choices: It added many extra cervical vertebrae
It still has seven cervical vertebrae, each greatly lengthened
The neck is one solid bone with no joints
questions.why: Like most mammals, a giraffe still has seven cervical vertebrae. Each bone is greatly lengthened — the neck did not gain a stack of extra bones.

questions.title: Scent
questions.stem: How do male giraffes check whether a female is ready to mate?
choices: They taste her urine (flehmen), sending cues toward the vomeronasal organ
questions.why: Males use the flehmen response: tasting a female’s urine to detect oestrus. The lip-curl routes chemical cues toward the vomeronasal organ.

questions.title: Gestation
questions.stem: About how long is giraffe pregnancy, and how many calves are usual?
choices: About two weeks; often a dozen calves
questions.why: Wikipedia gives gestation as about 400–460 days. Usually one calf is born; twins are rare. We keep that range rather than one exact day count.

questions.title: Evolution
questions.stem: What two main ideas does Wikipedia discuss for why giraffe necks became so long?
choices: Only swimming, with no other idea
Competing browsers reaching high food, and sexual selection via necking
Necks grew so giraffes could hibernate
questions.why: Wikipedia discusses both the competing-browsers idea (reaching food others cannot) and sexual selection (long necks helping males in necking contests). Scientists still debate which mattered more.

questions.title: Spots
questions.stem: What may the skin under a giraffe’s dark patches do besides camouflage?
choices: Store extra water like a camel hump
Hold complex blood vessels and large sweat glands that may help cool the body
questions.why: Wikipedia notes the skin under the dark blotches has complex blood-vessel systems and large sweat glands, which may help the giraffe regulate body temperature.

questions.title: Nerves
questions.stem: What is striking about a giraffe’s left recurrent laryngeal nerve?
choices: It is the shortest nerve in any mammal
It takes an extreme detour down the neck and back up, making it extraordinarily long
It only exists in baby giraffes
questions.why: In mammals the left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around a vessel near the heart, then returns to the larynx. In a giraffe that detour is extraordinarily long — a classic comparative-anatomy example.

questions.title: Society
questions.stem: How do giraffe social groups actually work?
choices: Purely random open herds with no lasting ties
Fission–fusion groups, with lasting female associations and kinship
Only solitary animals that never meet
questions.why: Giraffe groups were once called open and ever-changing. Newer work describes a fission–fusion society: groups split and join, but females often keep lasting associations and kinship ties.

african-elephant.source_note: Facts from Wikipedia, African elephant / Elephant.
talk_about: Why might a trunk be more useful than hands at the zoo?
If you had ears as big as an elephant’s, how would you stay cool?
Which other animal at the zoo lives in a family group?
push_further: An elephant’s trunk can grab, drink, and smell. What job would you give it first?
A herd follows the oldest female. Why might the oldest be a good leader?
Find one more big animal on your zoo map. How does it move if it cannot jump?

teach: The African elephant is the largest living land animal.
It eats plants — grass, leaves, and bark — not meat.
Its trunk can grab, drink, spray, and smell.
A baby elephant is a calf.
A herd is led by the oldest female.

questions.title: Biggest
questions.stem: What record does an African elephant hold among living land animals?
questions.why: The African elephant is the largest and heaviest living land animal.

questions.title: Food
questions.stem: What do African elephants eat?
questions.why: African elephants are herbivores. They eat plants such as grass, leaves, and bark — not meat.

questions.title: Trunk
questions.stem: What does an elephant use its trunk for?
choices: To grab, drink, spray, and smell
questions.why: The trunk is a long nose and upper lip. Elephants use it to grab food, drink, spray water, and smell.

questions.title: Ears
questions.stem: Why does an African elephant have such big ears?
questions.why: Big ears help an African elephant shed heat and stay cool.

questions.title: Young
questions.stem: What is a baby elephant called?
questions.why: A baby elephant is a calf.

questions.title: Family
questions.stem: Who usually leads an elephant herd?
questions.why: Elephant families live in a herd led by the oldest female, called the matriarch.

questions.title: Tusks
questions.stem: What are an elephant’s tusks?
questions.why: Tusks are very long teeth — not horns.

questions.title: Voice
questions.stem: What sound is an elephant famous for?
questions.why: An elephant’s famous call is a trumpet — a loud sound made through the trunk.

questions.title: Water
questions.stem: How can an African elephant swim?
choices: It can swim, and its trunk can act like a snorkel
questions.why: Elephants can swim. They sometimes swim underwater and use the trunk like a snorkel.

questions.title: Myth buster
questions.stem: Can an elephant jump?
questions.why: Elephants cannot jump. Their heavy bodies stay on the ground.

questions.title: Trunk
questions.stem: How is an elephant’s trunk built, muscle-wise?
choices: One long bone down the middle
Tens of thousands of muscles and no bone
A hollow tube of cartilage only
questions.why: The trunk is a muscular hydrostat — tens of thousands of muscles and no bone. Published counts vary, so we do not lock one exact number.

questions.title: Voice
questions.stem: How do elephants often talk across long distances?
choices: With low-frequency rumbles, many too low for humans to hear
questions.why: Elephants use infrasonic rumbles. Much of that communication is too low for humans, and it can travel far across the landscape.

questions.title: Gestation
questions.stem: About how long is African elephant pregnancy?
choices: About 22 months — the longest of any land mammal
questions.why: Calves are usually born after about 22 months. That is the longest pregnancy of any land mammal.

questions.title: Memory
questions.stem: Why can an older matriarch be especially important in a drought?
choices: Her memory of water and food can guide the family
She stores water in her tusks
questions.why: The oldest female leads the herd. Her long memory of where water and food were in hard years can help the family survive drought.

questions.title: Teeth
questions.stem: How do elephants replace worn chewing teeth?
choices: New molars move forward from the back, like a conveyor, several times in a lifetime
They grow a new set all at once each year
questions.why: Worn front molars drop out as new ones move forward from the back. Elephants replace these chewing teeth several times in a lifetime.

questions.title: Feet
questions.stem: Why can such a heavy animal walk so quietly?
choices: It has feathers on its feet
Fatty cushion pads under the feet help nearly silent steps
It walks only on its toenails
questions.why: Soft fatty cushion pads under the feet spread the weight and help an elephant walk with almost no sound.

questions.title: Smell
questions.stem: How strong is an elephant’s sense of smell?
choices: Among the best senses of smell of any mammal
Only as strong as a goldfish
questions.why: An elephant’s trunk is a powerful nose. Elephants rank among the mammals with the best sense of smell.

questions.title: Threats
questions.stem: What are the main threats to wild African elephants today?
choices: Elephants moving to the deep ocean
questions.why: The biggest threats are poaching for ivory and the loss and breakup of habitat.

questions.title: Compare
questions.stem: How can you usually tell an African elephant from an Asian elephant?
choices: African elephants have smaller ears and a rounded back
African elephants have larger ears and a concave (dipped) back
questions.why: African elephants typically have larger ears and a concave, dipped back. Asian elephants have smaller ears and a convex or level back.

questions.title: Myth buster
questions.stem: Are elephants really afraid of mice?
choices: Yes — they run from every mouse they see
No — that is a myth; they react to sudden movement, not mice specifically
questions.why: “Afraid of mice” is a cartoon myth. Elephants may startle at sudden movement near their feet, not at mice as a special fear.

questions.title: Species
questions.stem: How do scientists treat living African elephants today?
choices: Always one species forever, with no split
As two living species: bush/savanna Loxodonta africana and forest L. cyclotis
questions.why: Wikipedia treats living African elephants as two species — the bush or savanna elephant Loxodonta africana and the forest elephant L. cyclotis. IUCN assesses them separately. Status labels have shifted, so we do not lock one letter.

questions.title: Trunk
questions.stem: What is an elephant’s trunk, anatomically?
choices: A hollow bone like a horn
A fusion of the nose and the upper lip
Only a stretched nose, with no lip involved
questions.why: The trunk, or proboscis, is a prehensile elongation of the nose and upper lip. Those parts fuse in early development — it is not a nose alone.

questions.title: Trunk tip
questions.stem: How does an African elephant’s trunk tip differ from an Asian elephant’s?
choices: African elephants have no finger-like tip
African elephants have two finger-like processes; Asian elephants have one
questions.why: African elephants have two finger-like processes at the tip of the trunk. Asian elephants have one and more often wrap the trunk around food.

questions.title: Senses
questions.stem: How can elephants pick up distant seismic signals?
choices: They detect ground-borne vibrations through their feet and trunk
By tasting the air with their tusks
questions.why: Wikipedia notes elephants communicate with seismic vibrations that travel through the ground. They detect those ground-borne waves through the feet and the trunk.

questions.title: Musth
questions.stem: What happens when an adult bull elephant is in musth?
choices: Testosterone rises; he becomes more aggressive and sexually active, with temporal-gland signs
questions.why: Musth is a state in adult males: elevated testosterone, heightened aggression and sexual activity, plus temporal-gland secretions running down the face.

questions.title: Family
questions.stem: Who besides the mother often helps care for an elephant calf?
choices: Other young females in the family — allomothers
questions.why: Calves are cared for by their mother and other young females in the group, a pattern called allomothering or alloparenting.

questions.title: Teeth
questions.stem: What can happen after an old elephant’s last molar set wears out?
choices: The elephant may starve, because it can no longer grind plants well
questions.why: After the final molar set wears out, an old elephant may starve — a common late-life cause of death. The last replacement is the last.

questions.title: Digestion
questions.stem: How do African elephants digest tough plants?
choices: With a four-chamber ruminant stomach like a giraffe
By storing food in the tusks
questions.why: Fermentation of food takes place in the hindgut. Elephants are hindgut fermenters, not four-chamber ruminants like giraffes.

questions.title: Genes
questions.stem: What gene story is linked to elephants’ size and cancer resistance?
choices: They carry many copies of TP53, a gene linked to cancer resistance (Peto’s paradox)
They rely on extra hearts only
questions.why: Elephants carry many copies of the TP53 tumor-suppressor gene, which researchers link to unusually low cancer rates for such large, long-lived animals — Peto’s paradox. Published copy counts vary, so we do not lock one number.

questions.title: Seeds
questions.stem: Why are African elephants sometimes called megagardeners?
choices: They plant seeds with their tusks on purpose
They are long-distance seed dispersers; dung can carry many plant species
They only eat meat and never spread seeds
questions.why: Elephants are long-distance seed dispersers. Seeds pass through the gut and germinate in dung, which can carry many plant species — a megagardener role in the landscape.
